statement: A rectangle is longer than it is wide. In how many different ways can it be folded along a straight line so that the two halves match exactly?

choices.misconception: I thought only squares and circles can be folded so the halves match.
I found only the fold that goes up and down and missed the fold that goes across.
I counted the two middle folds and one corner-to-corner fold.
I thought the corner-to-corner folds work like they do on a square.

hints: Imagine folding a paper rectangle. Try the corners too.
A fold works only if every corner lands exactly on another corner. Test the fold through the middle each way, then test a fold from one corner to the opposite corner.
The folds through the middle, one up and down and one across, both work. Fold a long rectangle corner to corner and look at where the corners land.

solutions.reliable: Fold the rectangle in half the short way and the halves match. Fold it in half the long way and they match again. A fold from corner to corner does not work: the two triangles have the same size but the corners do not land on each other, because the sides are different lengths. So there are 2 ways. The idea to keep: a fold line works only when every point lands on a matching point.
solutions.elegant: A square has 4 fold lines because its sides are all equal. Stretching it into a rectangle breaks the two diagonal folds and keeps the two middle folds.

whyOnTest: The diagonal of a rectangle is the most common false line of symmetry, so this checks that symmetry is tested, not assumed.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
